overview: The Teams and Leagues cards were close to unanimous, and the sponsor cards were the hardest. More than half the Product Sponsors answers are brands like Toyota and McDonald's, which belong on Audience Sponsors.

Four students put Hawthorn on their map (players, coach Sam Mitchell, supporters, the team). They were following the sheet: its instructions named Hawthorn and Brisbane, written before the preliminary finals, and Fremantle made the Grand Final instead. One student also named Joe Daniher, who retired after the 2024 season.

Athletes → Fans was the most-drawn line at 28 answers, and 12 of those were the one word "entertainment." The money lines were thin: three answers on the whole sheet mention the broadcast rights fee, and none mention club memberships.

Students read the game through US sports. The centre bounce became a basketball tip-off, the Observations and Opinions boxes kept listing soccer, rugby and US football, and 14 questions were about the game growing, most often in the US.
The boxes disagree with each other. Some students saw constant fights and a confusing rulebook, and others saw smiling players who "do not fight" and rules that were "simple."

boxes.label: Observations
boxes.summary: Most students noticed three things: how physical the game is with almost no padding, how fast play restarts, and how packed and loud the stadium was. A second group watched the broadcast itself, the camera cuts, replays, score bug and commentary. And plenty of them reached for a US sport to explain what they saw, most often the basketball tip-off at the centre bounce.

boxes.gaps: Two sets of answers disagree: one group saw "lots of small fights" and "constantly bumping, tackling, and fighting," another saw players who "do not fight" and are "always smiling." And one student asked whether the Docker who went out of bounds was allowed to keep playing, which nobody answered; the ball has to be fully over the line, and a player standing out of bounds can still play a ball that's in.

boxes.label: Opinions
boxes.summary: The class split on whether the game is fun to watch or hard to follow, and a fair number said both in the same line. Almost everyone was taken with the fans. And a smaller group wrote about how the broadcast shapes the viewing, from who gets made into a main character to why the coaches barely appear.

themes.note: Constant action, high scores and a close finish kept them watching.

boxes.gaps: Students called the game "less rules" and "simple" in one place and "a lot of rules" and "confusing" in another, and nobody put the two side by side. And the opinion about goal-post hits is correct: a ball that hits the post scores a behind, one point.

boxes.label: Questions
boxes.summary: The biggest cluster asked whether the AFL could work outside Australia, and in the US in particular. Next came how the rules work and how the umpires keep up with 36 players. The money questions (player pay, ticket prices, what sponsors get back) and the broadcast questions (who picks the close-up, whether producers steer commentators) line up with the connections on the map.

themes.note: The US most of all, plus New Zealand, expansion past 18 teams, and a global audience.
examples: I wonder if this would be different if the rules were the same but the fanbase was US based

themes.note: Marks, free kicks, the 50-metre arc, scoring, when you can throw.
examples: I wonder if the game originated with all of the intricate rules (lengths to dribble, at what point you can throw, etc.) or if they have evolved and been added over time?

boxes.gaps: A few questions rest on a wrong fact. A goal is worth six points, not seven, and there are four posts, not three. The three-peat question has a fresh answer: this win was Brisbane's third premiership in a row, as they did in 2001, 2002 and 2003. And teams do go to the rooms at half time; the on-field huddles come at quarter time and three-quarter time.

cards.label: Teams

cards.label: Leagues

cards.gaps: "AFL Premiership" is the competition the league runs, not the league itself. The NFL, NBA and MLS entries came from one student who also wrote the AFL; they read as comparisons, but on this card they sit as if they were part of the AFL map.

cards.label: Governing Bodies
cards.summary: Most students found the AFL Commission, and one named its chair, Craig Drummond. Five wrote just "AFL," which puts the league and the governing body in the same box. Three put the umpires here.

examples: WAFC, AFL Comission

WAFC, AFL Comission
cards.gaps: "The AFL Commission (owns all the teams...)" is wrong: the clubs are member-owned, and the commission governs the competition. Umpires officiate games under the commission's rules, so they fit better with Staff than here.
